lesson.title: Two Roads, One Destination: Comparing Catalyzed and Uncatalyzed Pathways
lesson.summary: Placing the catalyzed and uncatalyzed energy diagrams for the same reaction side by side makes visible exactly what a catalyst does and does not change: identical reactants, identical products, identical delta H, but a dramatically lower energy barrier and often a completely different, multistep route in between.
lesson.body:
Bringing together the ideas from catalyst effect on Ea and energy diagrams, picture a single reaction coordinate diagram with two curves drawn on it for the same reaction. Both curves start at exactly the same point, the reactants' energy, and both end at exactly the same point, the products' energy, since delta H does not change with or without a catalyst. The uncatalyzed curve rises to one tall peak in between. The catalyzed curve, sharing those same two endpoints, instead rises through one or more much lower peaks, representing the intermediates of the catalyzed mechanism, before arriving at that identical final product energy.

The hydrogenation of ethene into ethane, C2H4 gas plus H2 gas forming C2H6 gas, is a good worked comparison. Uncatalyzed, this reaction between two gas molecules colliding directly has a very high activation energy, so high that at room temperature the reaction proceeds too slowly to observe, even though it is strongly exothermic and thermodynamically favorable, a case where a reaction that thermodynamics clearly favors is nonetheless blocked kinetically. Introduce a solid heterogeneous catalyst, finely divided nickel or palladium, and both H2 and C2H4 adsorb onto the metal surface, which weakens the H to H bond and the carbon to carbon double bond in ways that open a much lower energy, multistep pathway: adsorption, reaction on the surface, and desorption of ethane. With the catalyst present, the reaction proceeds readily at room temperature and moderate pressure. The reactants are the same, the products are the same, delta H is the same, strongly exothermic either way, yet the two rates are worlds apart, because the catalyzed route's highest point sits so much lower than the uncatalyzed route's single tall peak.

A short checklist captures what distinguishes a catalyzed diagram from an uncatalyzed one for the same reaction. The starting and ending energies are identical, so delta H is unchanged. The catalyzed pathway's highest point is lower, meaning both the forward and reverse activation energies are reduced by the same amount, consistent with the fact that equilibrium position is unaffected. The catalyzed pathway frequently shows more individual peaks and valleys than the uncatalyzed one, since it often proceeds through extra intermediate steps that the simpler, single step uncatalyzed mechanism never has. And only the rate differs between the two curves, never the destination.

This comparison is really the same idea from every angle explored across this unit. Mechanisms are built from elementary steps with one rate-determining bottleneck controlling the overall pace. Intermediates come and go without ever appearing in the overall equation. And a catalyst's entire job is to swap in a friendlier bottleneck, a set of smaller, easier steps in place of one large barrier, so that exactly the same chemistry, the same reactants turning into the same products with the same energy change, can occur, just far more quickly.
